results.why: K23 scores density of mathematical symbols, equations, asymptotic notation and variables, which is the same notational-density property as T01.

K15's cue list (theorems, proofs, convergence claims, bounds, regret rates, complexity statements) is essentially the same feature set that defines T02's learning-theory/optimization cluster, though K15 also credits bare mathematical notation and so would fire on some non-theory papers.

All four score the extent/prominence of code-and-data availability language counting both live or anonymised links and future release promises, which is exactly T03's boilerplate channel (K11 is excluded because it scores live-link versus promise as a contrast rather than presence).
No candidate scores passive-versus-active grammatical construction; the nearest, K08, scores first-person process narration against result-first framing, both of which are active voice.

K40 covers agreement errors, article slips, odd prepositions and awkward idiom as T05 does, but it explicitly requires ornate thesaurus-reaching diction to co-occur, so plain prose with grammatical slips would score much lower on K40 than on T05.
No candidate counts efficiency register (efficient, lightweight, scalable, fast, low-cost); the promotional-wording items K32, K44 and K46 track novelty and hype vocabulary instead.

K50 counts invocations of named large models, but it pools benchmarks, datasets and leaderboards into the same count, so an abstract naming only ImageNet/WMT would score high on K50 and zero on T07's checkpoint-enumeration channel.

No candidate scores applied-domain framing; K31 touches non-ML domains only as the zero pole of a much broader topic-crowding axis that also puts classical statistics and optimization at zero, and K49 scores urgency register rather than domain.
No candidate scores the habit of putting terms in quotation marks; the naming items (K16, K25, K26, K38, K39) score acronyms and brand names, and K28 scores bold/italic markup.

K04 is centred on priority rhetoric (claiming novelty, being first, setting records) but also counts superiority and state-of-the-art claims, which are common in abstracts making no first-ness assertion at all.

Both score lexical density of novelty-asserting adjectives with 'novel' and 'first' as leading exemplars, matching T11's word count, but each also pools in unrelated intensifiers (significant, comprehensive, robust, outperforms).

K28 scores how much bold, italic and emphasis markup appears in the text, which is T12's emphasis-practice channel (K02 and K36 are excluded because they score unrendered-source residue and paste-path layout damage).
